tip: 진짜 (jinjja = really) is the everyday casual version of 정말 (jeongmal), which sounds a touch more formal.
The word after 너무 (neomu) sets the tone: with 짜요 (jjayo = salty) it's a genuine 'too salty' complaint; before praise it would just mean 'so'.
시원해요 (siwonhaeyo = refreshing) – Koreans say it even about hot soup that hits the spot.
뜨거워요 (tteugeowoyo) = hot to the touch; spicy-hot is 매워요 (maewoyo).
맛없어요 (madeopseoyo = tastes bad) is 맛 (mat = taste) + 없어요 (eopseoyo = doesn't exist), run together as one word.
치킨 (chikin) usually means fried chicken; a live or raw bird is 닭 (dak).
One letter apart: 달라요 (dallayo) = different, 달아요 (darayo) = sweet. 맛이 조금 달라요 (masi jogeum dallayo) = the taste is a bit different, not a bit sweet.
Korean builds "need" from a noun: 필요 없어요 (piryo eopseoyo) is literally "necessity doesn't exist"; to need something is 필요해요 (piryohaeyo).
배불러요 (baebulleoyo = I'm full) is 배 (bae = belly) + 부르다 (bureuda = to be full), where 르 turns into 러. Say it after a good meal.
에서 (eseo) marks where an action happens: 앱에서 (aebeseo = on the app) pairs with 주문했어요 (jumunhaesseoyo = ordered). Plain 에 (e) normally marks a spot or destination, not an action.
그릇 (geureut = bowl) with native numbers: 두 그릇 (du geureut = two bowls).
비 (bi) on the end of a noun = fee: 배달비 (baedalbi = delivery fee).
Money uses Sino numbers: 삼천 원 (samcheon won = 3,000 won).
까지 (kkaji) stretches from 'up to' into 'even': 국물까지 (gungmulkkaji) = even the broth – all the way down the list to the last thing.
돼요? (dwaeyo? = does it work?) is the all-purpose 'can I / do you take': 카드 돼요? (kadeu dwaeyo?) covers 'do you take cards?' in two words.
돼요 (dwaeyo) is the all-purpose "it works / it's fine": 카드 돼요 (kadeu dwaeyo) = cards are accepted. Noun + 돼요? asks if anything is possible.
Bills "come out" in Korean: 얼마 나왔어요? (eolma nawasseoyo = how much is it?)
Korean counts in units of 만 (man = 10,000): 사만 원 (saman won = 40,000 won).
The -(으)ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) ending offers an action to the listener: 제가 계산할게요 (jega gyesanhalgeyo) = I'll get the bill – a volunteer move, not a prediction.
The -ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) ending is a promise to the listener: 살게요 (salgeyo) = "I'll buy – I've got this." Plain 살 거예요 (sal geoyeyo) just states a plan.
씨 (ssi) after a name is the polite default – 민수 씨 (Minsu ssi). It follows the given or full name, and you don't add it to your own.
괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo = it's fine) doubles as a polite "no thanks" – here it turns the receipt down.
값 (gap = cost) attaches to nouns: 저녁값 (jeonyeokgap = the dinner bill).
Double consonant matters: 쌌어요 (ssasseoyo) = was cheap, 샀어요 (sasseoyo) = bought. 싸다 (ssada = cheap) vs 사다 (sada = buy).
회식 (hoesik = team dinner) – after-work meals are a big part of Korean work life.
고기를 구웠어요 (gogireul guwosseoyo = grilled meat) – at a Korean barbecue the grill is set into your table and you cook the meat yourselves.
로 (ro = by) marks transport: 지하철로 (jihacheollo = by subway).
타다 (tada = ride) tags what you ride with 을/를: 지하철을 타요 (jihacheoreul tayo) – no separate word for "on" or "in".
몇 (myeot) + a counter asks 'which number': 몇 호선 (myeot hoseon) = 'what number line?'. The same 몇 also asks 'how many'.
Getting off happens at a place, so it takes 에서: 시청역에서 내려요 (sicheongyeogeseo naeryeoyo). 에서 marks where an action happens – plain 에 won't fit here.
